overview: Medieval Croatian kingship developed among communities whose lives survive in inscriptions, church buildings, tools and human remains. Royal titles and land grants show relationships between rulers and religious institutions; archaeology adds evidence of riding, food and health. The accession of an Arpad ruler in 1102 changed the dynasty while Croatian kingship and local society continued.

periods.title: Tomislav and the evidence for royal titles
periods.summary: Tomislav is called king in copies of papal correspondence associated with the Split councils. His reign is approximately dated, while a specific coronation ceremony and the full extent of his authority remain uncertain.

periods.title: Communities, writing and monastic patronage
periods.summary: Human remains illuminate life in communities such as Konjsko, while the Baska Tablet, carved around 1100, records a royal land grant and church building. These different sources reveal more than a succession of kings.

periods.title: Kingship under Coloman
periods.summary: Coloman was crowned king of Croatia and Dalmatia at Biograd in 1102. His recognition in Zadar followed in 1105. Royal continuity involved new rulers and negotiated or contested local relationships.

sections.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain

items.text: Tomislav's royal title survives through copies of papal letters associated with the Split councils, preserved in a much later compilation. The source tradition matters: a copied title is evidence to assess, not a surviving contemporary coronation record.

The familiar coronation at Duvno in 925 arose from later historical reconstruction. The Croatian Encyclopedia explains why that location claim was rejected and why a precise ceremony cannot be confidently reconstructed from the surviving evidence.

The Baska Tablet is a limestone slab originally belonging to the church screen at St Lucy's near Jurandvor on Krk. Carved around 1100, it placed a written record within a building used by a religious community.

Its text records King Zvonimir's gift of land, witnesses and an abbot's account of church construction. The inscription links property, prayer and patronage; damage and difficult readings prevent every personal name and clause from being treated as certain.

The tablet uses Croatian Church Slavonic and Glagolitic letters between rounded and angular forms. Its later reuse in the church floor damaged the surface. Both its script and its wear are part of the evidence for how the stone was used.

A bronze fitting from the cemetery near St George at Putalj was first catalogued as a Gothic buckle. Petrinec reidentified it as part of an early Carolingian spur set, dating to the late eighth or early ninth century.

The Putalj fitting has parallels in the Solin area and graves at Biskupija. It documents connections in riding equipment before the later royal-title evidence, but one imported style cannot establish every rider's birthplace or a whole community's identity.

Bone-collagen analysis at sites including Glavice-Gluvine and Radasinovci-Vinogradine suggests millet contributed to early medieval diets. This is a chemical inference about food consumed, not a surviving meal or proof that everyone followed the same menu.

The later Sibenik-Sveti Lovre sample differs from the other early medieval groups in that study. Its chemistry suggests a different protein mix, possibly including freshwater fish. The researchers' uncertainty is more informative than a single supposed national diet.

At the ninth- to eleventh-century Konjsko cemetery, researchers recorded dental and skeletal signs of stress and disease. Their comparisons help recover the lives of people absent from royal documents, while the small sample limits conclusions about the wider population.

St Mary's cartulary at Zadar records Coloman's 1102 coronation at Biograd. An inscription at St Mary's also supports Zadar's recognition of his rule in 1105, connecting written accounts with a surviving architectural setting.

Pacta conventa survives as a note appended to a manuscript from the 1380s. Most recent scholarship rejects it as an authentic contemporary treaty. A possible agreement with nobles should be distinguished from accepting this later text as its original record.

ending.text: In 1102 Coloman became king of Croatia and Dalmatia, bringing Croatian kingship under an Arpad ruler. This marks dynastic change rather than the extinction of Croatian society or the royal title. The terms of any contemporary agreement with nobles cannot simply be read from the much later Pacta conventa.

sources.title: Croatian Encyclopedia, Tomislav
sources.note: Royal title in copies of papal letters associated with the 925/928 councils; late manuscript transmission; nineteenth-century coronation reconstruction and modern rejection of the Duvno location claim. Early reign dates and borders remain uncertain.

sources.title: Croatian Encyclopedia, Bascanska ploca
sources.note: Opening description and final text analysis: limestone screen slab, approximate date around 1100, Croatian Church Slavonic, transitional Glagolitic letters, Zvonimir's land grant and church building. Damaged readings remain debated.

sources.title: Croatian Encyclopedia, Koloman
sources.note: 1102 coronation at Biograd recorded in St Mary's Zadar cartulary; royal titles; Zadar's recognition in 1105 and the church inscription. This is dynastic change, not the disappearance of Croatian kingship or society.

sources.title: Croatian Encyclopedia, Pacta conventa
sources.note: Note appended to a manuscript made in the 1380s; debate over authenticity and distinction between a possible agreement and an authentic contemporary treaty text.

sources.title: Maja Petrinec, A Bronze Loop of an Early Carolingian Spur Set from Putalj
sources.note: Archaeologia Adriatica 4 (2010), pp. 53-59, abstract: cemetery by St George above Kastel Sucurac, reidentification of the bronze fitting and late-eighth/early-ninth-century parallels. The object predates the tenth-century royal title evidence.

sources.title: Emma Lightfoot, Mario Slaus and Tamsin O'Connell, Changing cultures, changing cuisines
sources.note: American Journal of Physical Anthropology 148 (2012), pp. 543-556, DOI 10.1002/ajpa.22070; Table 1 and pp. 548-550: adult samples, early medieval millet interpretation and the distinct Sibenik-Sveti Lovre signal. Table A2 dates selected individuals; its dating ranges differ from the broad site labels, so no precise cemetery lifetime is adopted.

sources.title: Mario Novak and colleagues, Anthropological Analysis of the Konjsko polje/Livade Cemetery
sources.note: Starohrvatska prosvjeta III/35 (2008), English abstract and full study pp. 211-238: ninth- to eleventh-century cemetery, skeletal and dental stress, small sample limitations and uncertain hunting interpretation. Skeletal similarity is not used to assign biological ethnicity.
